name: Arugula
summary: Arugula is a fast-growing cool-season rosette harvested for peppery leaves. UW–Madison describes bolting under long days, heat or dry soil, repeat leaf harvest, and flea-beetle shot holes; its article uses Eruca sativa while Garden retains the accepted catalog name Eruca vesicaria.

identity.short: Catalog identity Eruca vesicaria; Extension also uses Eruca sativa
identity.guidance: Garden retains Eruca vesicaria as the accepted catalog identity. UW–Madison's article is titled Eruca sativa and notes E. vesicaria subsp. sativa as an alternative usage; this nomenclatural difference is recorded rather than silently changing the identity. No cultivar is represented.

growth.short: Rosette of lobed leaves; flowering stem can reach 2–3 feet
growth.guidance: UW–Madison describes a rosette of dull-green leaves, commonly 3–8 inches long. Long days, high temperatures and/or dry soil can trigger a branched flowering stem 2–3 feet tall. These are species/crop observations, not cultivar dimensions.

cultivation.short: Cool-season crop; full sun, with light shade sometimes slowing summer bolting
cultivation.guidance: UW–Madison recommends fertile, well-drained soil and full sun; light shade may slow bolting during the hottest part of the season. It also documents container growing, including a bright windowsill. These are outdoor/crop-level observations, not evidence for hydroponic performance or an artificial-light target.

care.short: Succession sowing can extend the supply of young leaves
care.guidance: UW–Madison describes sowing successive outdoor plantings every 2–3 weeks from early spring through fall for a continued supply, or allowing some plants to flower and self-seed. The schedule is regional outdoor guidance, not a year-round indoor production guarantee.

pruning.short: Cut leaves selectively or cut the rosette above the crown for regrowth
pruning.guidance: UW–Madison describes removing individual rosette leaves or cutting the whole plant 1–2 inches above the ground, followed by sequential harvest from regrowth. Use this as an outdoor crop option, not a guarantee of repeat regrowth in every system.

harvest.short: Harvest leaves a few inches long; heat and drought intensify flavor
harvest.guidance: UW–Madison says leaves can be picked at a few inches long; younger leaves are tender and peppery, while older leaves become stronger and more bitter. Whole plants may be cut after roughly 3–4 weeks in the described outdoor context, with sequential harvest from regrowth. Regular picking can delay seed-stalk development; heat and drought intensify flavor.

problems.short: Heat, long days and dry soil can trigger bolting; flea beetles leave shot holes
problems.guidance: UW–Madison links long days, heat and/or dry soil with rapid flowering-stem formation. Flea beetles can chew small shot holes and may severely damage young plants; row covers are described as an option, but beetles overwintering in soil may emerge beneath covers installed too early. Diagnose the actual symptom before intervention.

thinning.short: Outdoor spacing varies with individual-plant or cut-and-come-again harvest
thinning.guidance: UW–Madison gives 3–6 inches between individual plants and allows denser planting for cut-and-come-again harvest. These are field/container crop instructions, not a count of hydroponic pods or a universal indoor spacing rule.

hydroponics.short: Arugula is documented in NFT and research-scale DWC systems
hydroponics.guidance: Virginia Cooperative Extension lists arugula among salad greens that work well in nutrient-film technique (NFT). A University of Georgia greenhouse study also grew the named Slow Bolt selection in deep-water culture (DWC); this demonstrates crop/system use, not performance for every cultivar or consumer appliance. No pod count, machine fit, nutrient recipe, or EC target is inferred.

name: Rainbow Swiss Chard

care.short: Keep moisture even for continued leaf production; summer growth may slow

growth.short: Upright clump of dark leaves with thick white or light-green stalks
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes bok choy as an upright clump of dark-green leaves, each with a thick white or light-green stalk. This is crop-type morphology, not a named-cultivar size specification.

pruning.short: Remove outer leaves individually or cut the mature clump

name: Baby Spinach
summary: Baby spinach is a harvest stage/type of Spinacia oleracea, not a separate species or named cultivar. USU Extension describes spinach as a cool-season crop: heat and long days promote bolting and bitter flavor, while older leaves can be picked to let younger ones continue.

identity.short: Baby-leaf harvest type of Spinacia oleracea; no cultivar specified

growth.short: Leafy rosette; warm, long-day conditions encourage flowering
growth.guidance: USU Extension describes spinach as a cool-season leafy crop. Long days and warm summer temperatures can cause flowering and off-flavored or bitter leaves. This is species/crop-level behavior, not a claim about a specific slow-bolting cultivar.

cultivation.short: Cool-season growth in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture
cultivation.guidance: USU recommends fertile, well-drained soil and regular watering; moisture fluctuations can toughen leaves, slow development and contribute to off-flavors. The source's temperature and water amounts are outdoor Utah guidance, not indoor light or hydroponic nutrient targets.

care.short: Protect quality by avoiding heat and water stress
care.guidance: USU reports best growth below about 75°F and reduced quality, flowering and bitter/off flavors in high summer heat. Maintain steady moisture and control weeds with shallow cultivation; these are crop-level garden recommendations, not a system-specific climate recipe.

pruning.short: Remove older leaves without damaging the growing point
pruning.guidance: USU advises picking older leaves first so younger leaves continue growing; the whole leaf canopy can be cut close to the soil only if the growing point is not damaged. The source describes field spinach, so regrowth is not guaranteed in every container or system.

harvest.short: Pick usable leaves before the flower stalk forms
harvest.guidance: USU says individual leaves may be picked before the flower stalk forms, with older leaves removed first. The profile's baby-leaf label indicates intended harvest stage; the source does not define a single universal leaf size or harvest date for every baby-leaf planting.

problems.short: Heat/long days cause bolting; aphids, slugs and flea beetles leave clues

name: Roma Tomato

growth.short: Paste-type fruit is typically meatier and less juicy than other tomato classes
growth.guidance: Johnny's describes paste/plum/Roma as a broad class with typically meatier, less juicy fruit and processing uses. This is a type-level description, not a measurement or universal trait of every Roma-named variety.

cultivation.short: Grow in warmth and full sun after frost risk has passed
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension describes tomatoes as heat-loving, full-sun plants needing a long frost-free season. This is general outdoor tomato guidance; it does not establish a Roma-specific temperature, date, field spacing or indoor-light prescription.

care.guidance: UMN Extension links fluctuating soil moisture during tomato fruit growth with blossom-end rot and advises watering the soil rather than wetting leaves. This applies at crop scope in garden soil; no Roma-specific watering volume or hydroponic reservoir rule is inferred.

pruning.short: Choose support from the actual cultivar's growth habit
pruning.guidance: Johnny's offers determinate and indeterminate varieties within the paste/Roma class. Check the exact seed variety before deciding whether it needs staking or how to shape it; this profile does not prescribe one Roma-wide pruning or support rule.

harvest.short: Pick usable-size, usable-color fruit; mature-green fruit may ripen indoors
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension recommends harvesting tomatoes at usable size and color; many detach easily when ripe or nearly ripe, while some are cut from the plant in clusters. Pick remaining fruit when frost threatens. Fully developed mature-green fruit can often ripen indoors at room temperature, while truly green fruit may not ripen to good flavor. These are Minnesota home-garden crop cues, not a fixed calendar or cultivar-specific ripening guarantee.

problems.short: Recognize fruit disorders and leaf spots early
problems.guidance: On outdoor garden tomatoes, blossom-end rot appears as a tan-to-black flattened or scabbed patch at the blossom end; fluctuating soil moisture can contribute, and the symptom alone does not show that soil lacks calcium. Growth cracks may radiate from the stem or encircle fruit after rapid growth during heavy rain or heat, or after water returns following drought. Keep soil moisture steadier with regular root-zone watering and mulch. Brown-to-black leaf spots often start on lower leaves; early blight, Septoria, and bacterial spot can look alike at first. Keep foliage dry, improve airflow with support, remove spotted leaves early, and seek diagnosis before targeted treatment. UMN reports that larger slicer types are usually more prone to blossom-end rot than cherry types; this crop-type comparison does not establish this identity's susceptibility or resistance. This is outdoor garden guidance, not a hydroponic diagnosis.

flowering.short: Sustained heat can cause tomato flowers to drop before fruit set
flowering.guidance: UMN Extension reports that sustained heat above 85°F by day and 70°F at night can stress tomatoes and make flowers harder to pollinate during their roughly 50-hour pollination window; affected blossoms may dry, drop, and fail to set fruit. If flowers fall before fruit develops, compare recent day and night conditions. This is general outdoor tomato heat-response guidance, not a cultivar-specific tolerance rating or a diagnosis. The source notes that cooler nights can improve conditions for later flowers.

identity.short: Jalapeño Pepper identity is resolved at Capsicum annuum and Jalapeño type type scope
identity.guidance: This record represents the Jalapeño horticultural type within Capsicum annuum, not a named seed cultivar. Iowa State describes the type as small, blunt-oblong, thick-walled, and hot, with fresh and processed uses. UMN Extension specifically confirms that jalapeños can be harvested and eaten green; these type references do not establish a cultivar-specific size, heat value, or harvest date.

cultivation.short: Warmth and steady root-zone moisture support flowering and fruit set
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension reports that dry soil, daytime temperatures above 90°F, and nights below 60°F or above 70°F can weaken pepper growth in its Minnesota garden context. Maintain even root-zone moisture and avoid overhead sprinkling. Treat those temperature observations as regional outdoor guidance, not Jalapeño-specific thresholds or indoor/hydroponic setpoints.

care.short: Avoid excess nitrogen and protect healthy fruit-covering foliage
care.guidance: UMN Extension warns that excess nitrogen can produce leafy, bushy plants that bear fruit slowly. It also describes sunscald as pale, damaged patches on fruit exposed by an insufficient leaf canopy in hot, dry weather. Garden adaptation: avoid removing healthy leaves solely for appearance, and investigate nutrition or exposure before treating slow fruiting as a Jalapeño-specific defect. The source does not establish a fertilizer dose for pots or hydroponics.

pruning.short: Avoid removing foliage that shades developing peppers
pruning.guidance: UMN Extension links inadequate leaf cover with sunscald on exposed fruit during hot, dry weather. Preserve healthy canopy when pruning; remove damaged growth selectively and use support only if the actual plant needs it. This is a Garden adaptation from outdoor pepper guidance, not a cultivar-specific pruning schedule.

harvest.short: Jalapeños can be picked green once mature size is reached
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension says peppers may be harvested at mature size without waiting for red color, and specifically names jalapeños as usable while green. Clip the stem with clean, sharp shears when it does not release easily; continued picking allows the plant to keep flowering and setting fruit. Mature size and timing vary by the actual type and growing conditions, so this is not a fixed day-count promise.

uses.short: Usable fresh while green or ripe; also suited to processing
uses.guidance: Iowa State lists Jalapeño for fresh and processed use, and UMN Extension names it as a pepper that can be used while green. identity.short: Blue-flowered Borago officinalis; no named cultivar assigned
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Borago officinalis. Maryland Extension describes the species' sky-blue flowers; the catalog label 'Blue Borage' is treated as a flower-color type, not cultivar-level identity.

growth.short: Annual with coarse hairy leaves and star-shaped sky-blue flowers
growth.guidance: Maryland Extension describes coarse, hairy stems and leaves and sky-blue star-shaped flowers; plants reach about 2–3 ft in its garden guidance. NC State Extension lists a species-level height range of about 1 ft 7 in to 3 ft 2 in and a width of 1–1 ft 4 in. These are reference ranges for Borago officinalis, not guarantees for a named blue selection.

cultivation.short: Sunny, well-drained site; established plants readily reseed
cultivation.guidance: Maryland Extension recommends sunny, relatively dry places and notes that borage readily reseeds. NC State Extension says full sun is best but light shade is tolerated, and the species grows in varied soils including poor soil; it lists good drainage and occasional dryness. The combined guidance favors a sunny, well-drained site without claiming drought is required. Maryland also notes transplanting can be difficult; seed-starting details remain in the Seed Profile.

maintenance.short: Manage volunteer seedlings only if self-seeding is unwanted
maintenance.guidance: Maryland Extension reports that borage readily reseeds. Removing spent flower heads before seed development is a practical Garden adaptation only when volunteers are not wanted; leaving flowers supports the documented pollinator value.

harvest.short: Pick blossoms as they open; use leaves and flowers sparingly
harvest.guidance: Maryland Extension advises picking blossoms as they open and says leaves may be used fresh. It describes borage flowers and leaves for cucumber-like flavor in summer drinks. NC State Extension warns that edible leaves and flowers should be used only sparingly because liver damage can occur; no medicinal efficacy or Blue-cultivar-specific flavor claim is made.

problems.short: Powdery mildew can occur, though no specific pest problem is listed
problems.guidance: NC State Extension reports no specific insect or disease problems for Borago officinalis but notes that powdery mildew sometimes occurs. Treat this as a species-level observation, not a guarantee of resistance; inspect foliage if a white powdery coating appears and avoid diagnosing from appearance alone.

name: German Chamomile
summary: German chamomile (*Matricaria chamomilla*) is an annual with finely divided aromatic foliage and daisy-like flower heads. Wisconsin Extension recommends full sun and well-drained soil; harvest flower heads near full bloom for fresh or dried use. Deadheading can extend flowering, while allowing heads to set seed encourages self-seeding. Hydroponic fit remains unknown.

identity.short: Accepted species Matricaria chamomilla; distinct from other chamomiles
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Matricaria chamomilla and includes M. recutita in its synonym treatment. Wisconsin Extension cautions that several Asteraceae are called chamomile; pineappleweed (M. discoidea) lacks the white ray flowers around its yellow center, while Roman chamomile is Chamaemelum nobile. This profile is M. chamomilla, with no selected garden cultivar.

growth.short: Annual with branching stems and finely divided aromatic leaves
growth.guidance: Wisconsin Extension describes erect, branched stems, sparse finely divided leaves and shallow, spreading roots; its species-level outdoor account reports plants up to 2 ft tall. Flower heads have a domed yellow center surrounded by white ray flowers. Pineappleweed (M. discoidea) lacks those white ray flowers, so it is a distinct lookalike, not this identity. The height is not a named-cultivar or indoor-size guarantee.

cultivation.short: Full sun, well-drained soil and moisture in the upper root zone
cultivation.guidance: Wisconsin Extension recommends full sun and well-drained soil; the plant grows in poor soil and needs little fertilizer. Because its roots are shallow, irrigate as needed to keep upper soil moist but not wet. These are garden-soil recommendations, not hydroponic parameters.

maintenance.short: Deadhead to continue flowering, or leave heads to mature for self-seeding
maintenance.guidance: Wisconsin Extension reports flowering can continue until seeds ripen or frost when deadheaded and that plants readily self-seed if flower heads are not removed. Choose between continued bloom and allowing seed; this is an outdoor garden-management tradeoff.

harvest.short: Harvest flower heads near full bloom; use fresh or dried
harvest.guidance: Wisconsin Extension recommends harvesting flower heads when near full bloom for best quality, snipping the inflorescence from the stem; flowers may be used fresh or dried. This is species-level herbal/culinary use, not a medicinal efficacy claim.

problems.short: Aphids are a reported pest; few other pest problems are noted by Extension
problems.guidance: Wisconsin Extension reports few pest problems other than aphids in its garden account. This regional observation is not a universal pest-free or disease-resistance claim.
